entity: Acting Deputy Director, Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife
role: Acting Deputy Director, Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife
stance_basis: letter recommending exclusion of Bureau lands from ORV racing/rallies and more restrictive administration, while acknowledging the broader framework
summary: The Acting Deputy Director of the Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife submitted a memorandum commenting on the draft environmental statement for ORV use on public lands. The Bureau found the document generally comprehensive but raised specific concerns about ORV racing and competitive events on Bureau lands, inadequate noise standards, enforcement challenges, and misleading economic impact figures. The Bureau recommended that its lands be specifically excluded from competitive ORV events and that its administration of any ORV program be more restrictive than other bureaus given its primary wildlife protection mission.
complaint_summary: The Acting Deputy Director submitted a detailed memorandum raising eight specific concerns: the need to include all Executive Order definitions; the inconsistency of permitting ORV racing/rallies on Bureau lands with existing land management policies; a recommended rewording of the Bureau's mission description; misleading use of snowmobiling economic figures; suggested rewording of economic impact language; enforcement problems with posting only open areas; the need for specific decibel noise standards rather than vague 'unusual or excessive' language; and concerns about inconsistent open/closed policies across bureaus.

statement.text:
This Bureau appreciates the opportunity to review and comment on the subject draft statement pertaining to use of off-road vehicles on public lands. The document represents a comprehensive statement setting forth criteria for protection of natural resources on Federal lands. If the criteria are conscientiously followed and agencies carry out their mission responsibilities, adverse environmental effects should be minimized.
Our specific comments are as follows:
1. The proposal description should include all of the definitions as given in Section 2 of Executive Order 11644, unless a copy of the document is to be attached to the environmental statement. Of particular interest to the public would be the definitions of "off-road vehicles" and "public lands." Additionally, the statement does not mention ORV use on public lands which are open to mineral and mining entry and to established mining claims. The Executive order is not clear on this point; it is recommended that it be clarified in the statement.
2. The proposal to permit ORV racing, rallies, endurance contests, etc., on public lands is inconsistent with existing land management policies of this Bureau. It is recognized that the multiple-use concept is promoted when consistent with wise resource management. The broad authorization given to this proposal which will admittedly adversely affect the natural resources of this Bureau, in particular the National Wildlife Refuge System, is not responsible

management. Concessions such as this should be beyond the expectations of any user group. It is recommended that this Bureau be specifically excluded from participation in this activity by means of the draft environmental statement.
3. It is suggested that the paragraph concerning this Bureau (page 9) be reworded to read as follows: "The mission of the Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife is to assure maximum opportunity for the American people to benefit from fish and wildlife resources as part of their natural environment. The Bureau is responsible for the management and operation of a nationwide system of national wildlife refuges and waterfowl production areas comprising 30 million acres of land, including wilderness areas, 90 national fish hatcheries and 6 research stations along with associated lands. A significant portion of Bureau lands have been specifically designated as protected habitat for rare and endangered species of wildlife. Travel in or use of any motorized vehicle, including land, water, ice, snow, and aircraft types, is prohibited on areas administered by the Bureau of Sport Fisheries and Wildlife, except on specific routes of travel or in designated areas posted for public use. In accordance with paragraph 3(a)(4) of Executive Order 11644, areas and trails will be established only if the Bureau head determines that ORV use on Bureau lands will not adversely affect the natural, aesthetic, or scenic values. Because of the Bureau's primary responsibility for the protection and perpetuation of fish and wildlife resources, with wildlifeoriented public use as a secondary objective, administration of the ORV program must necessarily be more restrictive than other bureaus or agencies."
4. On page 17 it is stated that the Upper Great Lakes Regional Commission reported snowmobiling was worth $212,180,000 to the states of Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan in 1970-71. The Bureau feels it inappropriate to use this gross, or net figure without some follow-up discussion of associated impacts in terms of environmental degradation or possible human benefits received. Use of such an isolated figure as a beneficial impact only is misleading to the reader. Nuch of the description of economic impacts is inappropriate and unnecessary.
5. The last paragraph of page 17 is suggested for rewording as follows: "Controlled use, adequately administered, would have a minor alverse impact on the economic effects of ORVs. An enhancement of vacation land and home values is a possibility, but as yet is unproven. Environmental degradation could detract from previously established vacation land uses during the same or other seasons, and real estate values could actually decrease because of ORV intrusions and disturbances: Past off-season tourist periods could be eliminated or reduced. In individual areas where ORV use is prohibited, a negative impact would result."

6. While the Executive order and introductory statement of the draft refer to visually designating only those trails and areas open to ORV use, it should be readily recognized that posting only the open areas would pose enforcement problems. This is acknowledged in the environmental statement on page 20, line 13, which reads "...adequate posting must be improved to permit enforcement of any restrictions." In essence, this means areas not open should be posted. This may not be possible to do in some areas, and will require an expanded effort in communication, designation of areas, and enforcement.
7. We believe that completed studies on noise pollution contain enough information for definite acceptable noise levels to be spelled out (in decibels) for the different types of ORVs and outdoor public use areas. Included in the acceptable levels of noise must be the cumulative effect of several ORVs even though they are operating at their individual acceptable level. This determination must be made before adequate administrative controls can be developed—spice zoning, time zoning, restricted areas, etc. A general statement referring to "unusual or excessive" noise will not suffice because interpretation by individual land managers will vary and this will ultimately mean problems in administration.
8. Although we are aware of the problems that exist we feel there will be many problems regarding the open or closed policies of each of the Bureaus. They should be consistent.
It is hoped that the above will be helpful in preparation of the final document.
